mainTopic: Stopping a meal for תפלה; preparing for and prioritizing תפלה; when judging begins and ends; mealtimes; praying in a bathhouse
overview: The amud opens by finishing the question of why someone eating a meal must stop for ערבית but not for מנחה. It gives two reasons: drunkenness at night, and ערבית's long time window. רב ששת objects to the reasoning about loosening one's belt. The גמרא answers from the פסוק 'הכון לקראת אלהיך ישראל', which leads to stories about how אמוראים dressed for תפלה. Next come stories weighing תפלה against תלמוד תורה. The גמרא then defines when a דין begins, and it praises judges who judge truthfully even for one hour. It also discusses until what hour judges sit and the proper mealtime. Finally, רב אדא בר אהבה permits praying in a bathhouse. The גמרא challenges this and narrows it twice, and the last answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Drunkenness is rare by day but common at night
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why ערבית requires stopping a meal while מנחה does not: people rarely get drunk in the daytime, but often do at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: There (at מנחה), drunkenness is not common. Here (at ערבית), drunkenness is common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an earlier question: why do we make someone stop eating for ערבית but not for מנחה? The answer is that people tend to get drunk at night meals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that someone who keeps eating will get drunk and miss the תפלה. That risk is small at a daytime meal and large at a nighttime meal. So חז"ל made a stricter rule only for ערבית.

phrases.english: There (at Mincha), drunkenness is not common;
phrases.notes: People rarely drink heavily during the day.

phrases.english: here (at Arvit), drunkenness is common.
phrases.notes: Night meals often involve more drinking.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם לָא שְׁכִיחָא שִׁכְרוּת, הָכָא שְׁכִיחָא שִׁכְרוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised on the previous דף about the difference between מנחה and ערבית.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual distinction between the two cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since both are a meal before תפלה, they should have the same rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: Night meals carry a real risk of drunkenness, so a stricter rule was made only for ערבית.

steps.title: Second answer: a fixed time keeps a person alert
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: מנחה has a short, fixed time, so a person stays worried and remembers. ערבית lasts all night, so a person relaxes and forgets.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: with מנחה, since its time is fixed, a person is nervous about missing it and will not neglect it. With ערבית, since the whole night is its time, he is not nervous and will come to neglect it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different reason for the same difference between מנחה and ערבית. This one is about how people think, not about drinking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A short deadline makes people careful. A long window makes people say 'I have time' until they forget completely. That is why חז"ל were stricter about ערבית.

keyTerms.meaning: Alternatively; or you can also say

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a challenge to the first answer. אי נמי simply offers a second, separate reason for the same rule.

phrases.english: Alternatively: with Mincha,
since it has a fixed time,
he is anxious and will not come to be negligent.

phrases.aramaic: עַרְבִית — כֵּיוָן דְּכוּלֵּהּ לֵילְיָא זְמַן עַרְבִית,
phrases.english: Arvit: since the whole night is the time for Arvit,
he is not anxious and will come to be negligent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second explanation that replaces or adds to step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Psychological distinction between the two cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both תפלות should be treated the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: A long time window leads to forgetting, so ערבית needs extra protection.

steps.title: רב ששת: Is tying a belt really such a bother?
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת attacks the earlier idea that we let a person keep eating once he loosened his belt, because retying it would be a burden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת objected: Is it really a burden to tie his belt?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת challenges an idea from earlier in the סוגיא. That idea was that once someone loosened his belt, we do not make him stop, because it is a bother to tie it again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת says tying a belt is easy. It is too small a bother to justify skipping or delaying תפלה. So loosening the belt should not be a good reason to keep eating.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet objected to it:
Is it a burden to tie his belt?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question meaning: of course it is no real burden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the מנחה/ערבית difference to attack the reasoning about loosening the belt.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a loosened belt is a reason not to interrupt the meal
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Retying a belt takes almost no effort, so it cannot justify delaying תפלה.

steps.title: רב ששת adds: just pray without the belt
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת adds a second point: if retying is a bother, the person could simply pray without a belt.
steps.simpleTranslation: And more: let him stand that way and pray!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת adds another objection. Even if tying the belt were a bother, the person could pray without tying it, so there is still no reason to keep eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This argument assumes a belt is not needed for תפלה. If so, the belt has nothing to do with whether one should stop for תפלה. The next step will answer this by showing a belt is needed.

phrases.english: And furthermore, let him stand that way (without a belt) and pray!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, related challenge from רב ששת.
steps.kashyaTarget: The importance of the belt in this discussion
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a belt is not required for תפלה, he could pray without it, so the belt cannot be a reason to delay.

steps.title: A belt is needed: Prepare to greet your God
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a person must prepare himself properly for תפלה, based on the פסוק 'הכון לקראת אלהיך ישראל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it says: 'Prepare to greet your God, Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second objection. A person cannot pray without a belt, because the פסוק requires him to get ready and dress properly before standing before ה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wearing a belt is part of preparing for תפלה. So praying without one is not a proper option. This answers 'let him pray that way'.

keyTerms.meaning: Because it is said (in a פסוק)

steps.whyThisMatters: This פסוק becomes the source for preparing and dressing properly for תפלה, and it leads straight into the stories that follow.

phrases.english: Because it is stated:
"Prepare to greet your God, Israel" (Amos 4:12).
phrases.notes: One must get ready and dress properly before standing before ה'.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: הִכּוֹן לִקְרַאת אֱלֹהֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's 'let him pray that way' objection.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A belt is not needed for תפלה, so one could just pray without it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק requires proper preparation, so one may not pray without a belt.

steps.title: רבא בר רב הונא wore fine socks to pray
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב הונא would put on special socks for תפלה, based on 'הכון לקראת'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב הונא would put on (fancy) socks and pray. He said: 'Prepare to greet' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the גמרא just quoted 'הכון לקראת', it now tells how one אמורא acted on it. He dressed up, even his socks, for תפלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows one way to understand the פסוק: you honor the King by dressing nicely. The next stories will show a different approach.

phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Huna
would put on (fine) socks and pray,
he said: "Prepare to greet" etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא בַּר רַב הוּנָא רָמֵי פּוּזְמָקֵי וּמְצַלֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Associative: the פסוק from step 5 leads into a related practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dressing nicely for תפלה fulfills 'הכון לקראת אלהיך ישראל'.

steps.title: רבא prayed like a servant before his master
steps.stepSummary: רבא took the opposite approach. He removed his cloak and clasped his hands, showing humility like a servant.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא would take off his cloak, clasp his hands, and pray. He said: 'Like a servant before his master.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a contrasting practice. רבא prayed in a humble, submissive posture instead of dressing up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the focus is humility, not honor through clothing. A servant before his master does not show off; he stands humbly. Both approaches are ways of respecting ה' in תפלה.

keyTerms.meaning: Like a servant before his master

phrases.english: Rava would remove his cloak
and clasp his hands and pray.
He said: "Like a servant before his master."

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא שָׁדֵי גְּלִימֵיהּ וּפָכַר יְדֵיהּ וּמְצַלֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with רבא בר רב הונא's practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may pray in a humble posture, like a servant before his master.

steps.title: רב כהנא changed his style depending on the times
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי saw that רב כהנא prayed humbly in times of trouble and dressed up in times of peace, combining both approaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: I saw רב כהנא. When there was suffering in the world, he would take off his cloak, clasp his hands, and pray, saying 'Like a servant before his master.' When there was peace, he would dress, cover himself, wrap himself, and pray, saying 'Prepare to greet your God, Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the two practices can fit together. רב כהנא chose which one to follow based on what was happening in the world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In hard times a person begs like a servant, so humility fits. In good times a person comes to greet the King with honor, so fine clothing fits. The two approaches match two different situations.
steps.whatToRemember: Two ways to show respect in תפלה: dressing up (הכון לקראת) or humility (like a servant). רב כהנא used each one at its proper time.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
I saw Rav Kahana,
when there was suffering in the world,
he would remove his cloak, clasp his hands, and pray.
He said: "Like a servant before his master."
When there was peace,
he would dress, cover himself, wrap himself, and pray.
He said: "Prepare to greet your God, Israel."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: חֲזֵינָא לֵיהּ לְרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the two earlier practices together by applying each to a different situation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In times of trouble pray humbly; in times of peace dress respectfully.

steps.title: רבא criticizes רב המנונא's long prayer
steps.stepSummary: רבא saw רב המנונא praying at length and criticized him for leaving Torah (eternal life) for prayer (temporary life).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא saw רב המנונא making his prayer long. He said: They leave eternal life and busy themselves with temporary life.
steps.whatsHappening: Continuing the topic of תפלה, the גמרא tells how רבא criticized a long prayer. He felt the time should have gone to learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תורה is called 'eternal life' because it leads to עולם הבא. תפלה is mostly requests for this world's needs, so it is called 'temporary life'. רבא felt that lengthening תפלה takes time away from the greater value.

phrases.english: Rava saw Rav Hamnuna
who was prolonging his prayer.
He said: They abandon eternal life
and engage in temporary life.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא חַזְיֵיהּ לְרַב הַמְנוּנָא דְּקָא מַאֲרֵיךְ בִּצְלוֹתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New story, linked by the general topic of תפלה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבא, making תפלה long takes time away from תורה, which is greater.

steps.title: רב המנונא's view: תפלה and תורה have separate times
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רב המנונא's side: the time for תפלה and the time for תורה are separate, so a long prayer does not take from learning.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he (רב המנונא) held: the time for prayer is separate, and the time for Torah is separate.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב המנונא did not accept רבא's criticism. In his view, one is not taking time from Torah when praying at length.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא viewed all time as one pool, so more תפלה means less תורה. רב המנונא viewed them as two separate obligations, each with its own time. So each one gets its full due without competing.

keyTerms.meaning: And he held (was of the opinion)

phrases.english: And he (Rav Hamnuna) held
the time for prayer is separate
and the time for Torah is separate.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהוּא סָבַר זְמַן תְּפִלָּה לְחוּד וּזְמַן תּוֹרָה לְחוּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רב המנונא against רבא's criticism.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Conceptual explanation of the other side's view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Lengthening תפלה takes away from תורה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each has its own time, so a long תפלה does not take from תורה.

steps.title: רבי זירא rebukes רבי ירמיה for rushing to pray
steps.stepSummary: While learning with רבי זירא, רבי ירמיה rushed to finish so he could pray. רבי זירא quoted a פסוק against turning away from Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה was sitting before רבי זירא, and they were busy learning. The time for prayer was getting late, and רבי ירמיה was hurrying. רבי זירא applied this פסוק to him: 'One who turns his ear from hearing Torah, even his prayer is an abomination.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another story about תורה versus תפלה. רבי זירא criticized רבי ירמיה for hurrying away from learning in order to pray.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story leans toward רבא's view that תורה comes first. A prayer offered by someone who pushes away Torah is not accepted. The point is not that תפלה is unimportant, but that cutting Torah short for it is wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: A הלכה being studied, a Torah topic
It was getting late for praying

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה הֲוָה יָתֵיב קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya was sitting before Rabbi Zeira
and they were engaged in studying halakha.
It was getting late for praying,
and Rabbi Yirmeya was hurrying.
Rabbi Zeira read about him:
"One who turns away his ear from hearing Torah,
even his prayer is an abomination" (Proverbs 28:9).

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה הֲוָה יָתֵיב קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story on the same theme, supporting the priority of תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rushing away from Torah learning, even in order to pray, is criticized.

steps.title: When does a court case officially begin?
steps.stepSummary: Going back to the משנה, which says a judge who began a דין near מנחה need not stop, the גמרא asks when a דין counts as begun.
steps.simpleTranslation: From when is it the beginning of a court case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה's rule about starting a court case near מנחה. It is setting up the next move by asking exactly when a case is considered 'started'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that once the case has begun, the judges do not have to stop to pray. So we need to know the exact starting point. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The beginning of a court case

phrases.english: From when is the beginning of a trial?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the stories and returns to defining a term in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact moment a דין is considered to have started.

steps.title: Two opinions: judges wrapping or litigants speaking
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה and רבי יונה give two answers: the case begins when the judges wrap themselves, or when the litigants start their claims.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה and רבי יונה: One said, from when the judges wrap themselves (in their garments). The other said, from when the litigants begin to speak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two different answers to the question. Each אמורא names a different starting point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Judges used to wrap themselves in a טלית before judging, as a sign of seriousness. One view says this act starts the case. The other says the case starts only when the two sides begin presenting their claims.

keyTerms.meaning: The litigants (the two sides in the case)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yona (disagreed).
One said: from when the judges wrap themselves.
And one said: from when the litigants begin.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה וְרַבִּי יוֹנָה. חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12 with two opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either when the judges wrap themselves, or when the litigants open their claims.

steps.title: The two opinions describe different situations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes they do not argue. If the judges are already in the middle of judging, the next case starts when the litigants speak. If not, it starts when the judges wrap themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they do not disagree. This one is when they were already busy with a case. That one is when they were not already busy with a case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the two opinions do not really disagree. Each one is talking about a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the judges were already judging an earlier case, they are already wrapped, so wrapping cannot mark the start; the new case begins when the litigants speak. If the judges were not yet judging, the case begins when they wrap themselves.
steps.whatToRemember: A דין starts when the judges wrap themselves if they were not already judging. If they were already judging, the new case starts when the litigants open their claims.
steps.confusionAlert: The first הא (already busy judging) goes with the opinion about the litigants, not with the first opinion stated. The order is reversed.

phrases.english: And they do not disagree:
This (litigants beginning) is where they were already engaged in a trial;
phrases.notes: The judges are already wrapped, so the new case starts when the litigants speak.

phrases.english: that (judges wrapping) is where they were not already engaged in a trial.
phrases.notes: The wrapping itself marks the start of judging.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the apparent disagreement of step 13 by assigning each view to a different case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both opinions are correct, each for a different situation: wrapping marks the start for a new court session, and the litigants' claims mark the start for a court already in session.

steps.title: רב אמי and רב אסי call people in for judgment
steps.stepSummary: רב אמי and רב אסי learned near the door and kept inviting anyone with a case to come in.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אמי and רב אסי used to sit and learn between the pillars. Every hour they would knock on the door bolt and say: If anyone has a case, let him come in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about two sages who kept checking whether anyone needed a דין, even while they were learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story connects to the earlier discussion of judges and their duty. It shows that these sages treated judging as part of their job. They did not let their learning stop people from getting a דין.

phrases.english: Rav Ami and Rav Asi
would sit and learn between the pillars.
And every single hour
they would knock on the bolt of the door

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי: אִי אִיכָּא דְּאִית לֵיהּ דִּינָא,
phrases.english: and say: If there is anyone who has a case,
let him enter and come.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַמֵּי וְרַב אַסִּי הֲווֹ יָתְבִי וְגָרְסִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of judges from the discussion about when a דין begins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sages made themselves available to judge even while learning.

steps.title: Judges grow weak and are taught a verse about משה
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא judged all day and grew weak, so רב חייא בר רב מדפתי quoted a פסוק about משה judging from morning to evening.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא would sit in judgment all day, and they grew weak. רב חייא בר רב מדפתי taught them: "And the people stood over משה from the morning until the evening."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story and quotes a פסוק. This sets up the next move, where the פסוק will be questioned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two judges thought they had to judge all day, like the simple reading of the פסוק about משה. רב חייא brings this פסוק to show them that this is not what it means. The real explanation comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: Their hearts grew weak, from hunger

phrases.aramaic: רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
phrases.english: Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna
would sit in judgment all day,
and their hearts would grow weak.

phrases.aramaic: תְּנָא לְהוּ רַב חִיָּיא בַּר רַב מִדִּפְתִּי:
phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Rav from Difti taught them:
"And the people stood over Moshe
from the morning until the evening."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא הֲווֹ יָתְבִי בְּדִינָא כּוּלֵּי יוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about judges, this time judges who judged too long.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A פסוק seems to say משה judged all day.

steps.title: משה could not have judged all day
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks: if משה judged all day, when did he learn Torah?
steps.simpleTranslation: Could you really think that משה sat and judged the whole day? When would his Torah learning get done?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges the simple reading of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If משה judged from morning to night, he would have no time to learn. That cannot be true. So the פסוק must mean something else.

phrases.english: Could it enter your mind

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמּשֶׁה יוֹשֵׁב וְדָן כׇּל הַיּוֹם כּוּלּוֹ?
phrases.english: that Moshe sat and judged the entire day?
When would his Torah learning be done?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the simple reading of the פסוק just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading that משה judged all day.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Judging all day would leave no time for Torah, which is impossible for משה.

steps.title: Even one hour of true judgment counts like a full day
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק teaches that a judge who judges truthfully even for one hour is like a partner with הקדוש ברוך הוא in creation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק comes to tell you: any judge who judges a true judgment truthfully, even for one hour, the פסוק treats him as if he became a partner with הקדוש ברוך הוא in the creation of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the real meaning of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Morning until evening" is not a time count. It describes the value of true judgment. Even a short time judging honestly is credited like a whole day, so the judges do not need to starve themselves.

phrases.english: Rather, it is to tell you

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל דַּיָּין שֶׁדָּן דִּין אֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ,
phrases.english: any judge who judges a true judgment truthfully,
even for one hour,
the verse credits him

phrases.aramaic: כְּאִילּוּ נַעֲשָׂה שׁוּתָּף לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: as if he became a partner with the Holy One, Blessed be He
in the work of creation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by rereading the פסוק.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק describes the great value of true judgment, even for one hour.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why the judges in the story did not have to judge all day and grow weak.

steps.title: Linking משה's judging to the days of creation
steps.stepSummary: A גזרה שוה links "morning until evening" by משה to "evening and morning" in creation.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says here: "And the people stood over משה from the morning until the evening." And it says there: "And it was evening and it was morning, one day."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא proves the idea of partnership in creation from matching words in two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים use "morning" and "evening." Because the same words appear in creation, true judgment is connected to creation. That is the source for calling the judge a partner in creation.

keyTerms.meaning: A link between two פסוקים using the same word

phrases.english: It is written here:
"And the people stood over Moshe
from the morning until the evening."
And it is written there:
"And it was evening and it was morning, one day."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the claim in the previous step.
steps.raayaObject: A true judge is like a partner in creation.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The shared words "morning" and "evening" in שמות and בראשית.

steps.title: Until when do judges sit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what time judges normally stop judging.
steps.simpleTranslation: Until when do they sit in judgment?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new practical question: when does the court day end?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since judges do not need to judge all day, the גמרא wants to know the normal stopping time. This sets up רב ששת's answer.

phrases.english: Until when do they sit in judgment?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the idea that judges should not judge all day.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The normal time the court stops.

steps.title: Judges sit until mealtime
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת says judges sit until the time of the meal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: until mealtime.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers: the court ends at mealtime.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court day is limited by the meal. Judges sit in the morning, then stop to eat.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
Until mealtime.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question.

steps.title: A verse about ministers eating at the right time
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא brings a פסוק from קהלת: good ministers eat at the proper time, after the strength of Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חמא said: What is the פסוק? As it says: "Woe to you, land, whose king is a boy and whose ministers eat in the morning. Happy are you, land, whose king is free and whose ministers eat at the right time, in strength and not in drunkenness." In the strength of Torah, and not in the drinking of wine.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חמא gives a פסוק that hints to רב ששת's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bad leaders eat early in the morning instead of working. Good leaders eat "at the right time," after they have done the work of Torah and judgment. So judges first judge, and then eat.

phrases.english: Rav Chama said: What is the verse?
As it is written: "Woe to you, land, whose king is a boy
and your ministers eat in the morning.
Happy are you, land, whose king is free
and your ministers eat at the right time
in strength and not in drunkenness."
In the strength of Torah,
and not in the drinking of wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for רב ששת's answer.
steps.raayaSupportSource: קהלת י:טז-יז, ministers who eat at the right time after Torah.

steps.title: A list of who eats at which hour
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists the hours of the morning meal for different kinds of people.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: The first hour is when cannibals eat. The second is when robbers eat. The third is when heirs eat. The fourth is when workers eat. The fifth is when all people eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains what "mealtime" means for different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating very early is a sign of greed or idleness, like cannibals, robbers, or rich heirs with nothing to do. Working people eat later. Regular people eat at the fifth hour, according to this version.

keyTerms.meaning: Heirs who live off inherited money

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
The first hour is the eating time of cannibals.
The second is the eating time of robbers.
The third is the eating time of heirs.
The fourth is the eating time of workers.
The fifth is the eating time of all people.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שָׁעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה מַאֲכַל לוּדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the "mealtime" mentioned by רב ששת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Normal people eat at the fifth hour; workers at the fourth.

steps.title: רב פפא says the fourth hour is for everyone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא from רב פפא, who said the fourth hour is mealtime for all people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב פפא said: the fourth hour is mealtime for all people!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction between the ברייתא and רב פפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא put "all people" at the fifth hour. רב פפא puts them at the fourth. Both cannot be right as written.

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But Rav Pappa said
the fourth hour is mealtime for all people!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that all people eat at the fifth hour.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב פפא says all people eat at the fourth hour.

steps.title: The corrected list of eating hours
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the list: fourth hour for everyone, fifth for workers, sixth for תלמידי חכמים, and later is useless.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: the fourth hour is when all people eat. The fifth is when workers eat. The sixth is when תלמידי חכמים eat. After that, it is like throwing a stone into a barrel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the ברייתא so it matches רב פפא and adds what happens after the sixth hour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'All people' moves one hour earlier, from the fifth hour to the fourth. Workers move one hour later, from the fourth hour to the fifth. A new sixth hour is added for תלמידי חכמים, who are busy with Torah and judging until then. Eating after that does not help the body, like a stone tossed into a leather bag.

keyTerms.meaning: Like throwing a stone into a leather bag, meaning no benefit

phrases.english: Rather, the fourth hour is the eating time of all people.
The fifth is the eating time of workers.
The sixth is the eating time of Torah scholars.
From then on, it is like throwing a stone into a barrel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by correcting the ברייתא's text.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All people eat at the fifth hour.
steps.terutzMaskana: All people eat at the fourth hour; workers at the fifth; תלמידי חכמים at the sixth.
steps.confusionAlert: The original ברייתא is not kept as is. The גמרא replaces it with the corrected order, so learn the second list, not the first.

steps.title: Eating late is fine if you ate something in the morning
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the warning about eating after the sixth hour applies only if one ate nothing in the morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We only said this when he did not taste anything in the morning. But if he tasted something in the morning, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי limits the warning that eating after the sixth hour is useless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is going too long with an empty stomach. If a person ate a little in the morning, a late meal is still healthy. So the rule only applies to someone who fasted all morning.

keyTerms.meaning: We have no problem with it

steps.whatToRemember: Judges sit until mealtime. Even one hour of true judgment counts greatly. The corrected order: fourth hour for everyone, fifth for workers, sixth for תלמידי חכמים. Eating later is useless only if one ate nothing in the morning.

phrases.english: Abaye said: We only said this
when he did not taste anything in the morning,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל טְעֵים מִידֵּי בְּצַפְרָא — לֵית לַן בַּהּ.
phrases.english: but if he tasted something in the morning, we have no problem with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the last line of the corrected ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating after the sixth hour is only useless if nothing was eaten in the morning.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A small morning bite makes a late meal fine.

steps.title: A person may pray in a bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה rules that a person may say his תפלה in a bathhouse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: A person may pray his prayer in the bathhouse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It brings a ruling from רב אדא בר אהבה that one may pray in a bathhouse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bathhouse sounds like an unfit place for תפלה. That is because people are undressed there. רב אדא בר אהבה still allows it, and the rest of the סוגיא tests this surprising ruling.

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
A person may pray his prayer
in the bathhouse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It is loosely linked to the earlier discussion of when and how one prays.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Praying in a bathhouse is permitted.

steps.title: The three rooms of the bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא divides the bathhouse into three rooms. In the room where people stand naked, prayer is clearly forbidden. This contradicts רב אדא בר אהבה.
steps.simpleTranslation:
The ברייתא teaches about three rooms in a bathhouse.
Outer room (everyone is dressed): Torah reading and prayer are allowed. Greeting is surely allowed. One may put on תפילין, and surely need not take them off.
Middle room (some people are naked, some dressed): Greeting is allowed. Torah reading and prayer are not allowed. One need not take off תפילין he is already wearing, but he should not put them on there at the start.
Inner room (everyone is naked): Greeting is not allowed, and surely not Torah reading or prayer. One must take off his תפילין, and surely may not put them on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב אדא בר אהבה with a ברייתא. The ברייתא says prayer is forbidden in the bathhouse room where people are naked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain 'bathhouse' usually means the inner room where people actually bathe, naked. The ברייתא forbids even a greeting there, and all the more so prayer. That seems to directly contradict רב אדא בר אהבה, who allowed prayer in a bathhouse.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection, from a תנאי source
Greeting someone (saying 'שלום', which is a name of ה')
And needless to say (the more obvious case)
At the outset, from the start

steps.confusionAlert: The 'needless to say' order flips from room to room. In the outer room, greeting is the easier case: if even prayer is allowed, greeting surely is. In the inner room, prayer is the more obvious case: if even greeting is forbidden, prayer surely is.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One who enters the bathhouse,
a place where people stand dressed
there is Torah reading and prayer there.
And needless to say, greeting is allowed.
And he may put on tefillin,
and needless to say, he does not take them off.

phrases.aramaic: מָקוֹם שֶׁבְּנֵי אָדָם עוֹמְדִים עֲרוּמִּים וּלְבוּשִׁין
phrases.english: A place where people stand naked and dressed:
greeting is allowed there,
but there is no Torah reading or prayer there,
and he does not take off tefillin,
but he does not put them on at the outset.
A place where people stand naked:
greeting is not allowed there,
and needless to say, not Torah reading or prayer,
and he takes off tefillin,
and needless to say, he does not put them on!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אדא בר אהבה's permission to pray in a bathhouse.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא forbids prayer in the inner bathhouse room, which is the ordinary meaning of 'bathhouse.' This contradicts the permission.

steps.title: He meant an empty bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב אדא בר אהבה was talking about a bathhouse with no people in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב אדא בר אהבה said this, he meant a bathhouse with no people in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב אדא בר אהבה. It limits his ruling to a bathhouse that is empty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's problem is naked people being present. If nobody is there, that problem seems gone. So the permission and the ברייתא no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: When he said it (he meant in this case)
That has no person in it

phrases.aramaic: כִּי קָאָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה
phrases.english: When Rav Adda bar Ahava said it,
he meant a bathhouse with no person in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָאָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 28 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב אדא בר אהבה allowed praying in a normal, occupied bathhouse.
steps.terutzMaskana: He allowed it only in an empty bathhouse.

steps.title: A bathhouse is forbidden even when empty
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא taught that the forbidden bathhouse is forbidden even with no one inside, just like a bathroom without waste. This undoes the previous answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: The bathhouse the Sages spoke of is forbidden even if no one is in it. The bathroom they spoke of is forbidden even if there is no waste in it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks its own answer. It brings רבי יוסי בר חנינא, who says an empty bathhouse is still forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban does not depend on who is there right now. It depends on what the place is used for. A bathhouse, like a bathroom, is a disgusting place by its nature, so the 'empty bathhouse' answer fails.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? (introduces a challenge)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the principle that a place's main use defines its status for prayer, even when that use is not happening at the moment.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina say:
The bathhouse that the Sages spoke of

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אָדָם,
phrases.english: is forbidden even though there is no person in it;
the bathroom that the Sages spoke of

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ צוֹאָה!
phrases.english: is forbidden even though there is no waste in it!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 29.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that רב אדא בר אהבה meant an empty bathhouse.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוסי בר חנינא says a bathhouse is forbidden even when empty, so limiting the ruling to an empty bathhouse does not make prayer there permitted.

steps.title: רב אדא was talking about a brand-new bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: After the 'empty bathhouse' answer fails, the גמרא suggests that רב אדא בר אהבה permitted prayer only in a new bathhouse that was never used for bathing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רב אדא said it was allowed, he was talking about a new bathhouse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer to save רב אדא בר אהבה. He was talking about a brand-new bathhouse that no one has bathed in yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי בר חנינא taught that a used bathhouse stays forbidden even when it is empty, just like a bathroom with no waste in it. So the גמרא moves to a bathhouse that was never used at all. A place that was never used for its unclean purpose may not have that forbidden status.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the old answer and offers a new one)
In a new one (a bathhouse never yet used)
When he said it (introduces what the speaker really meant)

phrases.english: Rather, when Rav Adda said it,
phrases.notes: The word 'rather' signals that the previous answer (an empty bathhouse) is being dropped.

phrases.english: he meant a new one.
phrases.notes: This is a new bathhouse that no one has bathed in yet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer from Step 29, which Step 30 refuted, with a narrower case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the ruling is narrowed to a bathhouse that was never used.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רב אדא permitted prayer in an empty bathhouse, but רבי יוסי בר חנינא showed that a used bathhouse stays forbidden even when empty.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב אדא permitted prayer only in a new bathhouse that was never used for bathing.

steps.title: רבינא's unresolved question about a place designated as a bathroom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the 'new bathhouse' answer. רבינא asked whether a place merely designated as a bathroom is already forbidden, and that question was never resolved. The same doubt should apply to a new bathhouse, so how could רב אדא simply permit it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבינא asked: if someone designated a place to be a bathroom, what is the law? Does designating it count, or does designating it not count? The question was never answered. Isn't the same true for a bathhouse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the 'new bathhouse' answer. A new bathhouse has been set aside for bathing, and whether setting a place aside already makes it forbidden is an open question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא asked whether a place that was only designated as a bathroom, but never used, already has the forbidden status. That question stayed unresolved. A new bathhouse is the same kind of case, so it should also be in doubt and not clearly permitted as רב אדא ruled.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised a question (a real doubt, not an attack)
Designating a place for a certain use

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא's own question is a שאלה, a real doubt. Here the גמרא uses that doubt as a קשיא against רב אדא, because an unresolved doubt should not lead to a simple 'permitted' ruling.

phrases.english: But Ravina raised a question to him (Rav Adda):
phrases.notes: The word וְהָא ('but') signals a challenge.

phrases.english: if someone designated it as a bathroom, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The place was only set aside for this use and never actually used.

phrases.english: Does designation count, or does designation not count?
phrases.notes: Does setting the place aside already give it the forbidden status?

phrases.english: And it was not resolved for him.
Isn't the same true for a bathhouse?
phrases.notes: A new bathhouse was also designated but not yet used, so it should be in the same doubt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'new bathhouse' answer given in Step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that רב אדא permitted prayer in a new bathhouse.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whether designation alone creates the forbidden status is an unresolved doubt for a bathroom. The same doubt should apply to a new bathhouse, so רב אדא could not give a clear ruling permitting it.

steps.title: The answer begins: bathroom and bathhouse may be different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to reject the comparison between a bathroom and a bathhouse with 'No, perhaps'. The full explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, perhaps...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to answer the challenge by saying the two cases may not be the same. This line is only the setup, and the actual explanation comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word לָא ('no') rejects the claim that a bathhouse must follow the same law as a bathroom. The word דִּילְמָא ('perhaps') shows the גמרא will offer a possible difference between them. That difference has not been stated yet on this amud.

phrases.english: No, perhaps...
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the challenge from Step 32 by rejecting the comparison between a bathroom and a bathhouse.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between cases (the distinction itself appears on the next amud).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A designated bathhouse must share the unresolved doubt about a designated bathroom.
steps.terutzMaskana: Perhaps the two cases differ, so the bathroom doubt need not apply to a bathhouse. The details continue on the next amud.
